canberra.title: No Big Splash this summer, so Steel commissions a study
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government will try to flush out a buyer for the Big Splash site after its recent failed sale and the realisation that the lessee...
canberra.content:
Big Splash’s main pool was meant to reopen on 1 November, but the government believes that won’t happen. Photo: John Lomnicki.

The ACT Government will try to flush out a buyer for the Big Splash site after its recent failed sale and the realisation that the lessee won’t be able to reopen the site as required by 1 November, or any time over the summer.

The government will now commission, at taxpayers’ expense, an options study for the Macquarie site to provide information that may attract a buyer looking to set up a commercially viable operation, including an aquatic centre.

The year-long study will cover the practical costs of delivering various facilities, including slides, reopening pools and other amenities, as well as land value. It will analyse viable models for operating commercial aquatic facilities.

It will enable interested parties, including potential owner/operators, to come forward with ideas and plans about a future aquatic facility.

Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel said the report would also give the community a voice in future plans for Big Splash and inform the government’s aquatic study that was underway.

He said the government’s preference remained for a private operator to acquire the site, ruling out, for now at least, calls for a government takeover.

The government also had to be mindful of the current commercial arrangements which preclude it from constructing and/or operating new swimming pools, sporting or leisure venues within 5 km of the CISAC pool in Belconnen.

Mr Steel would not elaborate but said Access Canberra, as the regulator acting on behalf of the Territory Planning Authority, may also be considering action against the lessee for not meeting the 1 November opening requirement and the lease conditions.

He said the option study could help the lessee, which is the mortgagee and therefore with no interest in operating a pool or any other enterprise on the site, find a buyer.

Planning Minister Chris Steel said it’s important to know the actual costs. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Several other parties had expressed interest in the site, including the Canberra Southern Cross Club and the previous owners.

“It’s really important that as we consider the options for the future of Big Splash that we understand what the costs are,” he said.

“What are the costs of bringing the existing 50 metre pool back into operation? What are the costs of delivering new slide facilities, bringing back the amenities, and even delivering new facilities that weren’t provided there before?

“This report will give us those answers and enable, hopefully, the market and a potential operator to come in and run this as a successful and viable business, bringing it back as an aquatic facility.”

Mr Steel said interested parties could present their plans as part of the options analysis.

He committed to publishing the report so everyone could be clear about what was required to bring the site online as soon as possible.

But Mr Steel ruled out changing the site’s zoning from restricted access recreation zone PRZ2 to allow residential development.

“This is about looking at what’s possible within the current zoning,” he said.

“The range of different aquatic facilities that the community wants to see back on the site, looking at what the costs are of operating those and, potentially, delivering new facilities and what mix of facilities would make this commercially viable for an owner-operator to purchase the site and bring it back into operation.”

Asked about other possible recreational uses, Mr Steel said the community’s clear preference was for an aquatic centre.

The study will be funded from the City and Environment Directorate’s existing resources.

Asked if he was just throwing good money after bad, Mr Steel said the community wanted to have its say on the site’s future, and the government would provide that opportunity through this consultancy.

The expression of interest sales process run by Colliers concluded on 22 July without an outcome. The site attracted a lot of interest, but its “complexity” was an issue.

Canberra Liberals Member for Ginninderra Peter Cain said Mr Steel should examine all the possible ways Big Splash could reopen, including withdrawing the lease, but another report was not the way.

“Three weeks ago he told me that it should reopen by 1 November. Now he is commissioning another report. That is not enforcement. That is kicking the can down the road,” Mr Cain said.

“If he knew it could not reopen when he wrote to me on 25 August, he gave Belconnen false hope. If he didn’t, what was his guarantee worth?

“Enough reports. Enough threats. Take the lease back and secure Big Splash for Belconnen.”

Comment was sought from Save Big Splash.

canberra.title: Knife-wielding crim ferociously stabs man then leaves him on dirt road
canberra.snippet: Out of nowhere, Kalani Joliffe-Cole launched himself at a man and started repeatedly stabbing him in a frenzied attack. He then got back ...
canberra.content:
Kalani Joliffe-Cole, 29, has been sentenced to jail by the ACT Supreme Court. Photo: Facebook.

Out of nowhere, Kalani Joliffe-Cole launched himself at a man and started repeatedly stabbing him in a frenzied attack.

He then got back into a car and drove off, leaving his victim to bleed out on the side of the road from his life-threatening injuries.

Neither he nor any of the others in his car tried to help, and were it not for the assistance of good Samaritans who were driving nearby, the victim would likely have died.

Joliffe-Cole was found guilty of intentionally inflicting grievous bodily harm over the attack at the end of a jury trial, the ACT Supreme Court heard when he was sentenced on Tuesday (15 September).

Chief Justice Lucy McCallum said the victim had wanted to warn Joliffe-Cole’s friend that people were making threats against him, so he planned to meet him on 8 December 2022. But when the friend showed up, he found Joliffe-Cole had tagged along.

The victim thought his warnings were not being taken seriously and the others were being hostile to him. But he still drove with them to an associate’s house before the three men and two women all got into the car.

Joliffe-Cole drove the car to Uriarra Road, which is west of Canberra, before asking his friend, “Is this far enough?”

He pulled over to the side of a dirt road and told the victim to get out. Straight away, he hit the victim, then used a knife to repeatedly stab him in his head, chest, arms and back.

“The stabbing was repeated and ferocious,” Chief Justice McCallum said.

Joliffe-Cole got back in the car and drove the others away, leaving the bleeding victim alone in remote farmland with no phone or wallet.

Fortunately, drivers of two passing cars saw him. One provided first aid when he collapsed, while the other called Triple Zero.

A doctor thought the victim would have died without the urgent medical intervention he received.

As a result, Chief Justice McCallum said she wanted to acknowledge the courage and kindness of the people who stopped to help and the paramedics who acted quickly, because their actions likely saved his life.

During the trial, Joliffe-Cole claimed he acted in self-defence when the victim pulled out a gun. But the guilty verdict suggests the jury rejected this claim.

“There is no evidence he provided any threat whatsoever to the offender or [his friend],” Chief Justice McCallum said.

She said the others had remained in the car during the attack and hadn’t been charged as co-offenders.

The Chief Justice said the motive for the attack was unexplained, although she noted Joliffe-Cole was under the influence of methylamphetamine at the time.

She said he had suffered significant disadvantage in his childhood, which was a major factor that drove him towards drugs.

The father-of-two has been in continuous custody for about three years and eight months due to sentences he received in both NSW and in the ACT.

He was convicted and sentenced to a total of seven years and two months’ jail with a non-parole period of two-and-a-half years, backdated to account for time served.

Chief Justice McCallum said this may appear lenient, but it effectively means he will have been sentenced to a total of nine years and eight months’ jail, with a five-year non-parole period, when all his sentences from NSW and the ACT are combined.

Joliffe-Cole’s non-parole period means he will be eligible for release in January 2028.

But because he has an outstanding warrant for his arrest in NSW, authorities in that state will likely take him into custody again when he is released in the ACT.

canberra.title: Ex-cadet accused of leaving spy camera in ADFA bathroom hit with 260 charges
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged intimate image abuse. A former Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA) cadet accused of h...
canberra.content:
15 September 2026

Tain Stewart Stephens (insert) has been accused of hiding a camera inside the women’s bathrooms at the Australian Defence Force Academy (main image). Photos: Albert McKnight/James Coleman.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged intimate image abuse.

A former Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA) cadet accused of hiding a spy camera inside a bathroom at the Canberra facility now faces more than 260 charges over the allegations.

Region understands it is currently alleged the footage shows 46 different people.

ACT Policing previously alleged that a resident and staff members found a camera hidden inside a soap dispenser in a bathroom at the academy in May 2026.

When 20-year-old Tain Stewart Stephens was arrested over the discovery that same month, the ACT Magistrates Court heard police still had to examine 40,000 files as part of their investigation.

His matter returned to court on Tuesday (15 September), and the court heard police had laid an additional 181 charges against him.

Prosecutor James Melloy said the charges all arose from the same factual circumstances.

He said more than 250 charges had now been laid, while Mr Stephens had previously entered not guilty pleas to a number of them.

The courtroom was overseen by Special Magistrate Lucinda Wilson, the magistrate who granted bail for Mr Stephens in May.

“At his bail application I was told there was the possibility of further charges – and that has definitely happened,” she said.

Mr Stephens lives in Queensland and his lawyer, Angus Mackie-Williams of Hugo Law Group, said he had been excused from appearing in court in person if he was legally represented.

He asked for a 10-week adjournment for his team to consider the fresh charges and obtain instructions from their client.

Mr Mackie-Williams also asked for his client to be excused from appearing in person when the matter returned to court as it would be a great burden for him to travel to the ACT.

Special Magistrate Wilson said Mr Stephens should appear on the next occasion, but varied his bail to allow him to use the internet to appear in court via an audio-visual link.

He was previously banned from using the internet in general as part of his bail conditions.

The matter was adjourned to 24 October. No pleas were entered to the fresh charges.

In total, he has been charged with 222 counts of capturing visual data, 40 counts of possessing or controlling child abuse material and one count of using a carriage service to transmit sexual material without consent.

He is no longer a member of the Australian Defence Force.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on (02) 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on (02) 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to authorities by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: ACT looks to ban EFTPOS withdrawals at pokie venues to reduce gambling harm
canberra.snippet: Canberrans will no longer be able to withdraw cash through EFTPOS at poker machine venues, ATMs will follow, and every machine will event...
canberra.content:
Poker machine gambling harm is the target of the new legislation – but not all at once. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Canberrans will no longer be able to withdraw cash through EFTPOS at poker machine venues, ATMs will follow, and every machine will eventually require account-based gaming under a sweeping package of gambling reforms announced by the ACT Government.

The changes will also cut poker machine operating hours, simplify self-exclusion and progressively reduce authorised machines from just under 3500 to no more than 1000 by 2045.

But most changes will not happen immediately.

Gaming Reform Minister Marisa Paterson said reduced operating hours would begin on 1 July 2027, while legislation for the broader reforms would be introduced in October.

The EFTPOS withdrawal ban is expected to take effect within weeks of the legislation commencing; venues will have a year to remove ATMs, and mandatory account-based gaming will be rolled out over two years.

The government will also legislate a timetable requiring 500 poker machine authorisations to be removed every four years, reaching no more than 1000 across the Territory by 2045.

Dr Paterson said the package targeted gambling harm affecting more than 58,000 Canberrans, either directly or through a family member.

“We know that gambling harm, specifically from poker machines, is a major problem that our community faces,” she said.

Dr Paterson said multiple ATM withdrawals were the most commonly reported incidents on the Gambling and Racing Commissioner’s gambling incident register.

The existing deed-based self-exclusion process, which Dr Paterson described as “really onerous”, will also be replaced with a simpler legislative system, including an online option.

Poker machines will operate about 15 fewer hours each week, but gambling reform advocates say some safeguards in the package do not go far enough.

The Canberra Gambling Reform Alliance (CGRA) and ACT Council of Social Service (ACTCOSS) welcomed some measures, particularly the ban on cash withdrawals. But they warned the overall package was weaker than needed to adequately protect Canberrans from gambling harm.

They pointed to three major gaps: no legislated timeframes for breaks in play, no apparent mandatory loss limits, and shorter venue shutdown periods than previously promised.

ACTCOSS CEO Devin Bowles described removing ATMs and EFTPOS withdrawals as a “common-sense measure”, but said breaks in play were among the best-evidenced measures for reducing gambling harm.

“Canberrans are entitled to the protection they offer,” Dr Bowles said.

The organisations also want the government to release the technical advice behind its decision not to proceed with default load-up limits.

Relationships Australia lived experience advocate Markus Fischer with RA CEO Lauren Anthes and Gaming Reform Minister Marisa Paterson following the announcement of the ACT Government’s gambling reforms. Photo: Naziya Alvi.

CGRA co-chair Kate Seselja called the absence of loss limits an “enormous missed opportunity for better safeguarding”.

CGRA also wants the measures evaluated after 12 months.

“Some aspects of the proposed approach have not been implemented elsewhere so it is important we assess whether the interventions are actually working,” co-chair Jeremy Halcrow said.

The ACT Greens went further, accusing Labor of retreating from its previous commitment on poker machine operating hours.

Greens spokesperson for gambling harm Rebecca Vassarotti said Labor had promised in 2024 that venues would close between 2 am and 10 am, but the new plan would allow six additional operating hours each week compared with that commitment.

“Let’s be clear: nothing good happens in a poker machine venue at 3 o’clock in the morning,” she said.

Ms Vassarotti also argued pre-commitments or daily loss limits should follow gamblers between venues.

“Simply put, a Canberran could pick themselves up from the Hellenic Club, walk down the road to the Southern Cross Club and keep on betting.”

ClubsACT accepted that gambling harm needed to be addressed but warned restrictions on cash withdrawals could also affect spending on meals, raffles and entertainment, with flow-on consequences for clubs and the community activities they support.

It also argued the industry needed a realistic transition plan.

“You can’t cut off venue cash flow today and expect clubs to magically transform their business models tomorrow without a realistic, funded transition plan,” it said.

Dr Paterson said an independent inquiry and a joint transition council would help clubs diversify income, better use their land and assets and develop business models less reliant on gambling revenue.

“Ultimately, the fact that we have a club sector that’s reliant on revenue from gambling harm is not sustainable,” she said.

The ACT is also engaging with the NSW Government as it works on its own gambling reforms, including account-based gaming. Dr Paterson rejected concerns that tighter ACT rules would simply push gamblers across the border to Queanbeyan, pointing to reforms underway in NSW.

“This is not prohibition,” she said.

“You’ll still be able to play a poker machine in the ACT.”

canberra.title: Secrets of Canberra’s gardens open in exclusive tours this spring
canberra.snippet: Behind the hedge in a quiet Canberra street is a secret retreat, but its gates will soon open for visitors. Adrian Burton and his wife ha...
canberra.content:
Adrian says Forrest Bower draws from the “English cottage garden” and European formal garden traditions. Photos: Claire Sams.

Behind the hedge in a quiet Canberra street is a secret retreat, but its gates will soon open for visitors.

Adrian Burton and his wife have lived in their Forrest home for 25 years. Growing their garden, Forrest Bower, required every one of those years.

“We weren’t born gardeners, but we’ve always had an interest,” Adrian says.

“We both have very, very full-on jobs. I wanted to create something that would be a special environment for us to relax in.”

Adrian says they started with part of the block that was already established, before planting – and planning – the seeds for an expansion over time.

Forrest Bower is making its debut on this spring’s Open Garden schedule, supporting the Fred Hollows Foundation.

Open Garden was founded in 2015 and has since raised more than $100,000 for charity.

Once visitors walk through one of four gates at Forrest Bower, they enter a “woodland area” with young trees like cherries, crabapple, ginkgo and apricots.

“I love trees – if it’s just me, the whole garden would be an arboretum,” Adrian says.

“This is actually meant to be a shady, quiet and secluded area.”

A pathway leads to a terrace area with seating and a water fountain.

That area leads onto an open area, which Adrian says is intended as an events space.

“This is going to always be open, and because it’s open, you can get lots of bright flowers and your beautiful green grass,” he says.

A small selection of vegetables is planted at the back of the garden, near a compost station.

In creating the oasis, they draw from their early lives – including his 10 years living in France, while his wife was born in India and moved to England for her childhood.

“It’s the atmosphere, really, that is the theme,” he says.

“You can have trees and water in any sort of combination … But actually, it all comes down to what’s nice.”

Adrian: "My wife and I are very project-driven, so I think we get pretty bored sitting down for too long!"

Hidden among the different plants are souvenirs from their travels.

Adrian describes their approach to gardening as “conquering a very small territory” – one that comes with trial and error.

“We inherited some beautiful old trees – there are some 60-year-old trees on the block … We tried to knit it all together.

“If you just had a paddock and planted 100 roses, that’s not a garden. That’s a field.”

For Adrian, joining Open Gardens means more than letting people see what they’ve grown.

“We’re very conscious that we’re very lucky – actually very privileged – to have the space, the time [for the garden] … I’ve always had a little bit of a niggle in the back of my mind.

“Even though we’ve had an opportunity to really go for this garden and make it fabulous, we should give back to the community and share it.”

He is the first to say gardening takes time.

“I always find that you spend time in a spot, and then – all of a sudden – inspiration will come.

“You’ve got to have some kind of a plan. … You get to know where the sunshine comes in, or where people usually walk.

“The real inspiration comes after some time, and you say, ‘Ah, that’s going to work nicely’.”

Visit Open Gardens for more information on its spring season. Members have free entry to the gardens, while non-members pay an admission fee. Forrest Bower, at 13 Talbot Street in Forrest, will be open between 10 am and 4 pm on 19 September and 20 September.

australia.title: One of Sydney’s largest councils joins ban on ‘pervert’ glasses at local swimming pools
australia.snippet: Councillors say locals have been raising concerns about people secretly filming in change rooms, swimming pools and around schools Get ou...
australia.content:
One of Sydney’s largest councils has joined the City of Brisbane and the City of Yarra to issue a ban on AI smart glasses at public pools as concerns mount over the potential for predators to exploit the new technology.

On Tuesday evening, Canterbury-Bankstown voted overwhelmingly in favour of banning the tech at its pools, with its mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, describing them as “pervert glasses”.

Since their release, there have been reports of women being filmed without their consent and their interactions with a glasses-wearing influencer posted on social media.

“Chat groups, Facebook, local community forums and TikTok are just some of the online platforms where women are venting their concerns over the smart technology that threatens both safety and privacy,” El-Hayek told councillors at the meeting.

“Their biggest concerns are around ‘perverts and paedophiles’ secretly filming in change rooms, swimming pools and around schools.

“The latest AI smart glasses are wearable devices with high resolution cameras … and AI powered features like real time translation, object recognition and open-ear audio … these glasses can not only film, record and share footage, they can also scan your face and potentially access and retrieve information about you.”

Last month, Brisbane became the first council in Australia to publicly announce a ban on covert filming at its 21 public pools amid growing fears of threats to child safety.

The head of policy at Digital Rights Watch, Tom Sulston, praised the decision. He said it was “vital that councils across Australia ensure that public spaces like swimming pools are safe for families to enjoy without the threat of unwanted video surveillance”.

“We all need to be able to go out in public without fear of being covertly recorded and having the images uploaded to the internet without our consent,” he said. “We look forward to seeing not just councils following Brisbane’s lead, but also state and federal governments.”

Yarra in inner-Melbourne followed suit, voting last week to ban smart glasses from its leisure and aquatic facilities, childcare centres and playgrounds. It also confirmed it would call on the federal government to bring in stronger privacy laws to protect people from new technologies.

Randwick council in Sydney’s eastern suburbs has also banned the new technology at the Des Renford leisure centre. In a statement, it said “growing community concerns” about their potential misuse were behind the decision.

“Signage has been installed at the entrance and anyone wearing smart glasses in the centre will be asked to remove them or leave,” it said. “This precautionary measure will help ensure the centre remains a safe, welcoming and family-friendly place for all visitors.”

The bans will not apply to people with accessibility concerns, including vision impairment.

The federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, has not ruled out banning the glasses but has indicated how complex the laws are governing the new technology.

In August, she wrote to the privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, raising concerns she’d received from the community about their growing uptake and requesting it be given priority consideration.

“Privacy is an essential part of all our lives; it allows us to be who we are with dignity and without fear,” she said at the time.

“Unlike other forms of technology, smart glasses may be used more discreetly, making it harder to know when you are being recorded.

“The government is continuing to work on the next phase of privacy reforms to ensure our privacy laws are fit for purpose in the digital age.”

Australia’s online safety regulator has urged smart glasses companies to automatically blur people’s faces filmed on the devices, and make it clearer when someone is filming.

In advice to industry published at the end of August, the office of the eSafety commissioner warned that while smart glasses with cameras, such as Meta’s Ray-Ban, can offer accessibility benefits to low vision or blind people, companies might pit “accessibility benefits against safety and privacy considerations”, and noted there was already a backlash to the technology.

australia.title: Australia’s Indigenous population estimated at 2.2m before ‘demographic catastrophe’ of colonisation
australia.snippet: Study finds earlier numbers were underestimated, suggesting impact of diseases and massacres were much greater than previously thought Ge...
australia.content:
The number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia before colonisation was dramatically underestimated, according to new research that suggests many more of them were killed.

Modelling by a national research group puts the population levels before the 1788 first fleet arrived at 2.2 million, compared with early estimates of 250,000 people.

The research, by the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), has been published in the peer-reviewed Nature Human Behaviour.

The authors wrote that, historically, population estimates have been poor “due to lethal diseases, frontier and structural violence, and absence of systematic censuses” and that it’s “invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation” to try to rectify that.

They warn readers that the content of the study is confronting and possibly distressing.

The modelling showed there had to be millions of excess deaths from smallpox and other diseases, massacres, and the other results of colonisation such as dispossession and malnutrition, according to co-author Prof Corey Bradshaw, a global ecology professor at Flinders University.

His previous research found that an 1789 smallpox outbreak alone killed as many as 220,000 Aboriginal people. There were also other smallpox epidemics, as well as outbreaks of measles, influenza, tuberculosis, typhoid and other diseases.

Bradshaw said he would bet his career that massacre databases were underestimated by an “order of magnitude”.

“If you’re a frontier farmer, a colonialist that came out to a new area, and you were trying to remove people from ‘your’ land, you’re not going to write extensively about how many people you killed to do that,” he said.

“There’s another component here that’s essentially greed and racism – the entire concept of terra nullius was based on not many people being here. If there’s a systematic desire to take land [fewer people means a] better justification for imperialism.”

Australia was colonised on the basis of terra nullius, that it belonged to no one. That concept was overthrown with the high court’s Mabo decision, when it was recognised that First Nations people had been here for tens of thousands of years.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were not properly counted in the census until 1971, after the 1967 referendum. At that point, 115,953 people identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander.

In 2021, 812,728 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were counted in the census, a figure revised upwards to 983,257 with post-census recounts.

The estimate of 2.2 million, as well as a new estimate of 2.06 million excess deaths between 1788 and 1861, means the population was reduced to about 7% of its original size.

“We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonisation but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story,” distinguished professor Larissa Behrendt said. A Euahleyai/Gamillaroi woman, she is also the chair of the CIEHF’s advisory committee.

Early on after colonisation, various people estimated how many Aboriginal people were in their region. For example, governor Arthur Phillip estimated Gadigal people of the Eora nation came to about 1,500.

The first continent-wide estimate by social anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown put the number between 250,000 and 300,000, but mainly used observations from after the impacts of colonisation had been felt.

Radcliffe-Brown was aware that it was an underestimate, but many researchers since have relied on that count as a baseline. Again, they often recognised it would be an undercount because of historical reasons and changes in who identified or was identified as Aboriginal.

In 1983, economic historian Noel Butlin estimated the population at about 900,000. Later he increased that to between 1.1 million and 1.3 million. In 1987, archaeologists John Mulvaney and J Peter White argued it was more likely 750,000.

There have been many and varied estimates since, usually based on historical and ethnographic information.

The Australian team used different approaches to model the population. They looked at archaeological items to reconstruct how many people would have been there at a particular time, reconstructed the climate and the productivity of the land to infer how many people it could sustain and looked at genetic data to work back in time based on known DNA mutation rates.

They also reviewed, but did not rely on, ethnographic estimates.

“The findings highlight the scale of demographic catastrophe experienced by Indigenous Australians due to colonisation, with the implications being a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma and to inform future policy that assists Indigenous people,” said co-author and distinguished professor Lynette Russell of the Monash University Indigenous Studies Centre and CIEHF.

The authors wrote that Australia must prioritise reconciliation, engagement and policymaking with Indigenous people who still suffer intergenerational trauma and that the broader community should embrace the rich culture that survived these events.

The lead author, James Cook University associate professor Alan Williams, said the “devastating findings” highlighted the impacts of invasion. However, they also demonstrated the “remarkable survival, resilience and recovery over the past century of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island people”.

Behrendt said the research “tells us something extraordinary”.

“Our survival is one of Australian history’s most remarkable stories,” she said.
