    Welcome

What we learned, Tuesday 15 September

Achol Arok

That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today!

Before we go, let’s take a look at the day’s top headlines:

  • Pauline Hanson has offered a qualified apology for her comments about Indigenous Australians and about Anthony Albanese’s mother – both which have been widely condemned.

  • Chris Bowen has watered down any expectations that a renewed rise in oil prices will lead to the reintroduction of the federal government’s fuel excise relief.

  • Clare O’Neil has defended her colleague, the transport minister Catherine King, after it was revealed the latter had accepted a lifetime membership to Qantas’s top-tier membership, the platinum Frequent Flyer rewards.

  • Independent MP and former Winter Olympian Zali Steggall has joined the chorus of criticism against an ad for a US sports wagering company featuring actor Sydney Sweeney.

  • Universities Australia has warned One Nation’s plan to drastically cut down international student numbers will lead to campuses shutting down and domestic students missing out.

  • The National Disability Insurance Agency has announced voluntary redundancies for the first time since its creation in 2013.

  • Queensland’s state government has flagged a new crackdown in the state’s parole system under legislation introduced into state parliament today.

  • “Activists” and “green groups” will be banned from objecting to Queensland mining projects, under new legislation introduced into parliament today.

  • Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif has fronted the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption after an explosive appearance on Monday.

  • The Gold Coast mayor, Tom Tate, swore at an ABC journalist before storming out of a press conference after a series of questions about his trip to Mar-a-Lago to spruik an ultimately doomed $1.5bn plan for a Trump hotel on the Gold Coast.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning.

Australian fashion brands Cue and Veronika Maine face collapse

Longtime Australian fashion brands Cue and Veronika Maine are facing collapse after being placed under the control of receivers and managers.

The company’s parent said the decision followed “a difficult period”.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Hilco Capital said:

It is a disappointing outcome, but the only available course of action given the circumstances.

Our intention has always been to fund Cue to restore growth and profitability. This appointment will now provide an opportunity for a new owner to carry the Cue and Veronika Maine brands forward.

I want to acknowledge the efforts of all the staff during a challenging period and thank them for their continuing support of these great Australian fashion brands.

Human Rights Commission condemns Hanson’s comments about Indigenous Australians

The Australian Human Rights Commission has joined widespread condemnation of Pauline Hanson’s offensive comments about Indigenous Australians.

The commission said the comments contradicted Australia’s shared values of “fairness, dignity and respect” and had “no place in the national conversation”.

The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander social justice commissioner, Katie Kiss, said:

Such commentary is a tactic to divide us at a time when we need to come together. In fact, people have come together over the past 24 hours, across the political spectrum, to criticise the senator’s comments.

For that, I am heartened. But the harm caused should not be underestimated.

The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, added:

Whether our ancestors arrived more than 200 years ago, or we are recent migrants, we all live on lands and waters that were maintained by and hold the cultures of First Peoples. Recognising that gives us strength and brings us together. Denigrating First Peoples does the opposite and lessens all of us.

When public figures use language that dehumanises entire groups of people, it causes real harm. History has shown that when people are portrayed as less deserving of dignity, respect or belonging, discrimination and exclusion are more likely to follow.

Sivaraman said the incident reinforced the commission’s recommendation in the National Anti-Racism Framework for anti-racism training for all parliamentarians.

Three-year-old girl dies after being hit by car in Sydney’s west

A three-year-old child has died after being hit by a car in Auburn, in Sydney’s west, on Tuesday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to Normanby Road at about 2.05pm following reports that a child had been struck by a vehicle entering a driveway.

Paramedics treated the girl at the scene before taking her to Westmead hospital in a critical condition. She later died from her injuries.

Police said the 27-year-old male driver was not injured but was taken to Auburn hospital for mandatory testing.

An investigation into the circumstances remains under way.

King accuses Hanson of ‘gaslighting’ Indigenous Australians and prime minister

The resources minister, Madeleine King, has accused the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, of “gaslighting” Indigenous Australians and the prime minister after Hanson offered a qualified apology for comments that have been widely condemned.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, King said Hanson’s apology was inadequate. She said:

There is a way of apologising, isn’t there? … ‘Sorry if I caused offence’ is not really an apology.

She says outrageous things about Indigenous Australians, disgusting things, and then walks back into this building and says she did not say it at all. That is gaslighting.

What she said about the prime minister’s much-loved mother is beyond the pale, and a pseudo-apology is just pathetic on her behalf.

NSW police watchdog delays public examinations into alleged protest brutality investigation

The NSW independent police watchdog, the law enforcement conduct commission (Lecc), has delayed public examinations into its investigation of alleged police brutality, citing “a range of procedural issues”.

In February, the Lecc launched Operation Makalu to investigate allegations arising from violent clashes between police and demonstrators at a protest against the visit of the Israeli president, Isaac Herzog.

The delay comes two weeks after the leak of police body-worn camera footage of the protest, which was shared widely on social media. The footage allegedly shows a male police officer telling colleagues during a 9 February protest at Sydney Town Hall: “I fucking pumped that cunt.”

The commission has not specified when the public examinations will begin.

In a statement, the Lecc said:

The Commission had previously announced that any public examinations would start no earlier than September 2026. A range of procedural issues have now arisen, which the Commission must consider. As a result, public examinations will not be held in September 2026.

The Commission will provide a further update on its investigation as soon as practicable.

Two WA teens charged after alleged Perth Zoo break-in

Western Australia Police have charged two teenage boys after an alleged break-in at Perth Zoo during which a crocodile was assaulted and property was damaged.

Police allege the boys, aged 16 and 17, entered the zoo at about 7.15pm on Sunday. It remains unclear how they gained entry.

The teenagers allegedly cut the locks on a crocodile enclosure before entering and striking the animal with a metal pole. They are also accused of damaging CCTV equipment inside the enclosure by removing the cameras from the wall.

The incident was reported to authorities the following morning, before police arrested the teenagers at their separate homes.

Both boys have been charged with two counts of criminal damage or destruction of property, one count of trespass and one count of animal cruelty.

Andrew Messenger

State politicians react to Guardian story about man Tasered in homeless clearance

Queensland politicians have reacted to Guardian reporting that a man was Tasered in a homeless clearance earlier in the month.

The man attempted to kill himself after being ordered to leave a park north of Brisbane to make way for a kite festival. He was rushed to hospital, but discharged the next day.

The opposition leader, Steven Miles, said the state government had “washed their hands of responsibility for the homelessness crisis that they’re contributing to”, blaming cuts to the state’s emergency fund for accommodation in hotels and motels. He said.

We’re seeing this situation get even worse. It’s pretty much every park across Moreton Bay, whether that’s Pelican Park in Redcliffe, all the way through to Fernie Grove, there’s more and more people popping up in those parks.

Miles said it wasn’t appropriate for a hospital to discharge a patient back into homelessness.

Greens MP Michael Berkman said the case was “the end result of both major parties treating housing as a profitable commodity rather than a human right”. He said:

Our Government has created this vicious merry-go-round by underfunding housing, healthcare and community services.

If this is how the system treats a homeless man with terminal illness, it makes you wonder how they’re treating other people who we just haven’t heard about.

The minister for correctional services, Laura Gerber, said she wasn’t familiar with the case but said the government prioritised community safety.

Gold Coast mayor tells journalist to ‘fuck off’ during press conference

Andrew Messenger

Gold Coast mayor Tom Tate has sworn at an ABC journalist before storming out of a press conference.

ABC reporter Liam Walsh asked Tate a series of questions about his trip to Mar-a-Lago to spruik an ultimately doomed $1.5bn plan for a Trump hotel on the Gold Coast.

Tate claimed to have met with the US president at his golf estate at the invitation of the Trump organisation – but no record of the invitation exists, the ABC said.

Walsh asked Tate on Tuesday how much the trip cost. The mayor responded that “it’s private” and denied he got “mate’s rates”.

Then the mayor asked the reporter why he was so aggressive and if he was with the ABC, which the reporter confirmed.

“Fuck off,” Tate said, and walked out of the press conference.

The hotel plan fell over in May, with the developer claiming the Trump brand was too “toxic” to work with.

Achol Arok

Good afternoon!

I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of the afternoon’s news.

Krishani Dhanji

Thank you all so much for joining me on the blog today!

I’ll leave you with the fabulous Achol Arok and see you here bright and early tomorrow.

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • The opposition picked a broad bunch of questions (and was perhaps a bit all over the place) to target Labor with today, from the Whyalla steelworks, to a fundraising dinner attended by Albanese, to green hydrogen, to private health insurance rebates for over-65s.

  • Albanese defended Australia’s democracy and his government’s transparency, in response to a question from Allegra Spender. His answer was essentially: well, at least it’s not as bad as it is overseas.

  • The prime minister also said it was appropriate that a Labor staffer, and ex-Play School host, was stood down after old tweets disparaging Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and others were revealed.

  • The opposition then tried and failed to table photographs of the staffer in question with Albanese.

  • And Jim Chalmers defended Australia’s debt to GDP ratio with a line that boiled down to: well, it’s not as bad as it is overseas (… sound familiar?).

  • Angus Taylor didn’t get a question in today, and no MPs were kicked out despite a somewhat loud and at times rowdy 75 minutes.

Nassif threatens to pull out from Icac hearings mid-rant

Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif has threatened to withdraw from the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s inquiries as the counsel assisting attempted to interrupt a rant about corrupt politicians.

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC asked him to calm down, but Nassif quickly snapped back.

Dialling into the inquiry from Lebanon, he said:

“I want to prove my point. If you don’t want me to prove myself I’ll withdraw from all this nonsense.”

Showing his handwritten notes to the camera, Nassif said:

I’m taking notes … So stop fucking putting words in my mouth. This is a public hearing, and I know what you’re doing. You want to show the public that I am corrupt. I’m not corrupt.

You guys are not attacking the corrupt officials in the government. You want the country to be ruled by crooks.

Assistant commissioner Fabian Gleeson SC told Nassif to take a breath:

“The purpose of this inquiry is to get to the truth of certain allegations. It’s not for you to attack other people. You can be passionate about that, but this is not the forum for those complaints.”

‘I am not corrupt’: Jean Nassif declares innocence

Kat Wong

Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif is fronting the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption to wrap up his evidence after an explosive appearance on Monday.

Nassif told the commission he offered lobbyists Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis $1m to help fast-track his developments.

As counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC read texts between Greenwood and Ellis about Charles Perrottet not prioritising the developments, Nassif said he did not understand what this had to do with him.

Dialling in from his Beirut bedroom, Nassif said:

This is an issue amongst them and between them. I was not involved at all. I am not involved with paying politicians to get my projects approved.

I employed consultants to solve my problems and unblock the way …

What they did, if they did any corrupt work, I am not involved with it. I was not aware of it … You need to understand. I am not corrupt.

As part of its investigation into allegations against people associated with the NSW Liberals, Icac is examining the allegation that Liberal figures anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited donations from Nassif in exchange for political outcomes, including damage to the career of the NSW Liberal minister David Elliott, and the removal of the building commissioner David Chandler.

Nassif has denied wrongdoing.

QT ends without question from opposition leader

After a final dixer, the prime minister calls time on QT for the day.

We’re halfway through folks.

Interestingly, Angus Taylor didn’t ask a single question today.

Australia’s gross debt-to-GDP ratio lower than any major advanced economy, Chalmers says

One Nation MP David Farley is next from the crossbench and asks if the treasurer will accept “commonwealth debt has reached a point beyond which it becomes unsustainable? Yes, or no? If yes – what gross debt-to-GDP ratio or what gross debt level would trigger that concern with you?”

Jim Chalmers says Australia’s debt-to-GDP ratio isn’t that bad compared with other countries, and that much of the debt was accrued during the Coalition government.

We have lower gross debt-to-GDP than any major advanced economy – in fact, much lower. Less than half the US, UK, less than a quarter of Japan. That’s really important because, to go to the core of his question, there are other countries where debt is approaching unsustainable levels, but not in Australia.

Farley tries to make a point of order, saying Chalmers isn’t answering the question about what debt level would cause concern.

Chalmers continues:

If you look at US bond yields, Treasury yields, for 10 years, they’ve breached 5% again today. That is a source of considerable concern for policymakers and decision-makers, governments, and the private sector right around the world. And it reflects a number of things. It reflects the fact that the war in Iran is dragging on longer than anyone would like from an economic point of view.

Immediate action taken against Labor staffer Muldoon ‘appropriate’, PM says

Anthony Albanese says it is “appropriate” that Labor senator Richard Dowling has stood down ex-Play School host Rhys Muldoon as his staffer.

Tweets by Muldoon about Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and Peta Credlin were unearthed today, leading to the “immediate action” – as Albanese put it – taken against him.

Nationals MP Anne Webster asked Albanese when he first became aware of Muldoon’s “vile tweets”.

Albanese won’t give a timeline.

When they became public debate today – I wasn’t aware of those comments until they were raised in the media – and neither was Senator Dowling. The comments are completely unacceptable, and Senator Dowling has taken immediate action – and that’s appropriate.

Liberal frontbencher Aaron Violi tries to table a series of documents including: “the Prime Minister, on election night, with his close personal friend Rhys Muldoon. The Prime Minister being kissed on the cheek by his close political ally Rhys Muldoon. And disgraced Labor adviser Rhys Muldoon with the Prime Minister.”

Milton Dick is absolutely not having that, and warns Violi “don’t take advantage of my goodwill or the House’s goodwill by using props to try and table things.”

‘I’ll meet with leaders who have never held a press conference’: Albanese defends his government’s transparency

Will the government commit to publishing ministerial diaries, or lists of who ministers have met, so Australians can see who really is in the room, asks Allegra Spender.

She quotes a survey conducted by McKinnon which found “72% of Australians think politicians serve ourselves and vested interests first, before we serve them”.

Albanese says that his diary is regularly published via FOI requests – but what Spender is suggesting is the proactive publishing of all ministerial diaries.

He then defends the current system and says at least Australia is, like, better than other countries.

When I go to the UN next week, I’ll meet with leaders who have never answered a question in parliament. I’ll meet with leaders. I’ll meet with leaders who have never held a press conference and answered questions from journalists. In most parts of the world, leaders do not go through the transparency that we have in this country. So I’m proud of our democracy.

Albanese mentions the national anti-corruption commission which has never held a public hearing and the independent parliamentary standards commission (whose work is also shielded from public scrutiny).

australia.title: ‘Mafia boys’ and ‘corrupt politicians’: fugitive developer Jean Nassif rants to Icac from Beirut bedroom
australia.snippet: Nassif declares ‘I’m not corrupt’, threatens to pull out of evidence and waves handwritten notes at counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer Follow ...
australia.content:
Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif has declared he is “not corrupt”, claimed his daughter was forced to plead guilty to fraud and threatened to take the New South Wales government to The Hague in an explosive appearance at the state’s corruption watchdog.

Dialling into the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry from his Beirut bedroom, Nassif, 58, said he would return to Australia when he clears his name.

His evidence was part of an investigation into allegations against people associated with the NSW Liberals, where Icac is examining whether Liberal figures anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited donations from Nassif, in exchange for political outcomes including damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister David Elliott and the removal of then-building commissioner David Chandler.

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC on Tuesday asked why Nassif had left Australia in December 2022 and whether he was attempting to avoid giving evidence at a parliamentary inquiry.

But Nassif batted away the suggestion, claiming he had travelled overseas to accept an international award.

He said he later chose to stay overseas because he was receiving threatening messages, but vowed to return to Australia in the future.

“I was planning to run – at the international court from [The Hague] – to sue the government,” he said.

“I’m going to collect the beautiful legal team who are willing to fight politicians to clear my name and when that court case is finished, I’ll be back in Australia.

“I’m not gonna go back to Australia to be killed by mafia boys.”

Nassif also said he had “lost his mind” after he and his family were “attacked” by politicians and the media.

“I will go back to Australia and I will make sure they all go to prison for what they did to my family, especially my daughter,” he told Icac.

His 32-year-old daughter Ashlyn Nassif was sentenced to a six month community corrections order earlier in September after pleading guilty to providing false or misleading information to obtain a $150m construction loan from Westpac.

Her lawyers argued she had succumbed to pressure from her father when she falsified the documents.

But her father claimed she was “forced” to plead guilty.

“They’re corruptly damaging a diligent … young, smart, beautiful, hard-working, honest girl because of their dirty mind and corrupt thinking,” Nassif said.

“My daughter has been forced to plead guilty so she can finish that case … but the police could not get any evidence of wrongdoing.”

Throughout his evidence, Nassif launched into multiple rants about NSW politicsand the state of the construction industry.

He claimed Elliot had delayed approvals to put pressure on him, accused the building commissioner of lying about defects in his buildings, and said he was “fed up with the budget and the way the government is ruled by corrupt politicians”.

Dwyer repeatedly urged Nassif to remain calm, asked him not to shout at her, and tried to pose further questions, but the property developer would not be stopped.

Showing handwritten notes to the camera, Nassif said: “I’m taking notes … so stop fucking putting words in my mouth. This is a public hearing, and I know what you’re doing. You want to show the public that I am corrupt. I’m not corrupt.”

The assistant commissioner Fabian Gleeson SC told Nassif to take a breath.

“The purpose of this inquiry is to get to the truth of certain allegations,” Gleeson said.

“It’s not for you to attack other people. You can be passionate about that, but this is not the forum for those complaints.”

Nassif responded by saying: “No, no, no, no. There is no one [who] can make me shut up. If you guys are not going to accept the problem, I need to pull out now.”

Nassif initially appeared at Icac on Monday. He produced a medical certificate to excuse himself from a scheduled appearance earlier this month.

australia.title: Labor staffer and former Play School host sacked for ‘abhorrent’ posts attacking Peta Credlin
australia.snippet: Rhys Muldoon uses X to target Tony Abbott’s former chief of staff and senator Jacinta Price The Labor party has stood down a former Play ...
australia.content:
The Labor party has stood down a former Play School host turned ALP staffer for social media posts in which he referred to News24 host Peta Credlin as “a strap on wearing fantasy for Liberals”.

Rhys Muldoon was on Tuesday stood down from his position in Tasmanian senator Richard Dowling’s office after news.com.au first reported the comments.

In 2022, Muldoon used X to make a string of sexist attacks on Credlin, the former chief of staff to Tony Abbott, writing: “She’s what Liberals think of Margaret Thatcher. They picture her with a strap on, pounding away at their sorry a**ses”. The account has since been deleted.

Guardian Australia has seen screenshots of the posts before they were deleted. Muldoon has been contacted for comment.

“The tragedy of Peta Credlin … is her belief that anyone other than fetishised old white men think she contributes anything apart from a compromised boner”, he wrote in another.

In a 2023 post he described Country Liberal senator Jacinta Price as a “quisling” – a traitor who collaborates with enemies – because she did not support the voice to parliament.

News.com.au reported he used the N-word in a 2014 post making fun of Australian legal protection for free speech.

On Tuesday, Dowling said he had stood down the staffer after he became aware of the comments.

“After being alerted to abhorrent tweets from my staffer, I’ve decided to not continue with his casual contract,” he told Guardian Australia in a statement.

“Everyone in public life has a responsibility to do better when it comes to political discourse. The words used were unacceptable at any time.”

Muldoon was a guest at the wedding of prime minister Anthony Albanese and Jodie Haydon, appeared in the TV sitcom Us and Them and, with Kevin Rudd, co-authored a children’s book called Jasper and Abby and the Great Australia Day Kerfuffle. The prime minister’s office was contacted for comment.

In parliament, Albanese said it was “appropriate” that the staffer was stood down.

“When they became public debate today, I wasn’t aware of those comments until they were raised in the media, and neither was Senator Dowling,” he said.

“The comments are completely unacceptable, and Senator Dowling has taken immediate action – and that’s appropriate.”

Speaking to Guardian Australia, Credlin questioned how Muldoon was cleared by ALP vetters.

“I was surprised that someone with that sort of social media history got through Labor’s vetting net and got a job in the first place,” she said.

“I’m pretty disgusted that he was a star guest at the prime minister’s wedding. But it says more about this individual than it does about me.”

world.title: ‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US
world.snippet: Drive to save thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of ‘white genocide’ appears to show signs of slowing When Donald Trump announced ...
world.content:
When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.

However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in South Africa.

After Trump’s February 2025 executive order announcing the resettlement programme, which was expanded to include members of a “racial minority”, the first group of 68 white South Africans arrived in the US that May. The US also shut down the refugee programme for anyone else fleeing war and persecution.

Since then, more than 13,000 have moved to the US, according to state department figures. Arrivals are also accelerating, with more than 2,600 admitted in August.

Afrikaners, descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime repressed the black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.

Since the end of apartheid more than 30 years ago, affirmative action policies have helped to create a black elite and middle class. But about 38% of black South Africans are unemployed, compared with 9% of white South Africans, according to official data.

Meanwhile, the “black economic empowerment” policies, along with high crime rates that affect everyone, have fostered a feeling among some white South Africans that they are now the victims of racial discrimination.

The racist far right has also long highlighted brutal murders of white South African farmers, claiming them as evidence of white people being targeted. Official crime data does not show farmers or white people experiencing crime at higher rates. That has not stopped Trump amplifying these claims, in the face of the South African government’s furious rebuttals.

On 30 June, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for prospective and successful refugee applicants began to light up with news that people had begun to receive rejection letters.

“We are writing to inform you that, following review, USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] found your application to be ineligible for continued processing for resettlement to the United States at this time. This cannot be appealed,” the letters said, according to multiple rejections seen by the Guardian.

It is unclear how many have been found ineligible. USCIS did not provide data on the total number of refugee applications and rejections. One WhatsApp group set up to support rejects, called Hope beyond the Letter, had 311 members as of 10 September, according to one of the administrators, who noted that the membership fluctuated.

While the ineligibility letters did not give reasons for rejection, some applicants were given more information after making Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. The WhatsApp group administrator, a 64-year-old freelance TV professional, who did not want his identity disclosed, found that his case was initially “recommended for approval”. However, the recommendation was reversed because his ex-girlfriend, whom he had applied with, had a marijuana conviction.

“I cried like a baby,” he said, of receiving the rejection letter on 30 June, having finished the screening process in November. “It was something I actually believed was attainable. I believed the hype.”

Pieter and Liesl (not their real names) were told they were “conditionally approved” as refugees last November. Both are Afrikaners who had a grandparent killed on a farm and were managing a farm when they applied to become refugees.

Pieter said he was convicted of trespassing in 2014, for which he said he paid a fine and did not go to court. He was granted multiple temporary visas to work on farms in the US between 2011 and 2024.

The couple’s youngest daughter was born in the US and is a US citizen. In the response to their FoI request, they noticed that USCIS had recorded her nationality as South African and incorrectly said that she would be left behind if they moved to the US as refugees.

They had already sold their house, car and many of their possessions when they received a rejection letter on 24 July. “We have to start all over again,” Pieter said.

Another applicant blamed not being able to speak in his native Afrikaans for what he claimed were misunderstandings that led to him and his wife being rejected. The reasons given in response to their FoI request were “crime involving moral turpitude” and “commission of acts of torture or extra judicial killing”.

The 67-year-old had admitted to shooting at least one black person when working as a security guard in 1995, but said it was in self-defence while responding to the mass break-in of an alcohol shop. “I was thoroughly investigated by the authorities,” he said. “I was not charged, because I did not break the law.”

In an emailed response that did not address specific cases, the USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said: “The Department of Homeland Security is committed to resettling Afrikaner refugees who are being persecuted by the South African government.

“[USCIS] reviews each refugee application on a case-by-case basis … [and] notifies aliens found ineligible for continued processing through the US Refugee Admissions Program, including those found ineligible for public safety concerns or criminal histories. This cannot be appealed. This administration will always prioritize the safety and welfare of the American people.”

world.title: Ebola outbreak in DRC has peaked, say authorities, as infection rates slow
world.snippet: Almost 3,500 people have died in outbreak and experts say more must be done to ensure Bundibugyo is under control Authorities in the Demo...
world.content:
Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have announced that the Ebola outbreak ravaging parts of the country has reached its peak.

For the first time since the epidemic was declared in May, the numbers of people becoming infected is slowing down, according to officials.

Stressing that strict adherence to preventive measures needed to be kept in place, Samuel Roger Kamba, the Congolese health minister, said there was a decline in transmission of the Bundibugyo variant of Ebola.

“We are fighting a very dangerous virus that is killing many of our people. Today, we can say that the outbreak is under control,” he said. “At one point, we were recording about 120 cases per day; today, we’re seeing about 80 per day. So the number of new cases is decreasing every day.

“It has been more than 22 days since 10 of the 62 health zones have reported new cases. And so we can now definitively remove six health zones from the list because they have gone more than 42 days without new cases, and we can remove four health zones that have gone more than 21 days without a new case,” Kamba said.

Last week, the Sud-Ubangi region, on the DRC’s borders with Congo-Brazzaville and Central African Republic, became the sixth province to report the disease.

The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared by Congolese authorities on 15 May and is concentrated primarily in Ituri province, where ongoing conflict has created challenging conditions for those responding to the disease. It is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in the DRC since the highly contagious disease was first identified and named in 1976.

No effective treatment for the Bundibugyo variant has been found so far but there are clinical trials in the region. The DRC received more than 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine last month, which is the only approved treatment for the more common Zaire Ebola virus.

According to the latest data from the Congolese health ministry, the number of confirmed cases stood at more than 7,200, including more than 3,475 deaths, as of 14 September.

While welcoming the progress made, Iracan Gratien de Saint-Nicolas, an MP for Bunia, warned against what he called “triumphalism” and stressed that efforts must intensify to show people that the disease was under control.

Gratien Iracan called for lessons to be learned from failures in epidemiological surveillance that contributed to the rapid spread of the disease.

The MP also expressed some scepticism over the government announcement. “Claims that an epidemic is under control must be supported by objective indicators. If the indicators show that the epidemic is indeed under control, let’s make them public. Transparency in the data will strengthen public confidence,” he said.

He warned that some indicators that showed an epidemic was under control seemed to have been omitted by the DRC authorities, such as a sustained decline in new cases (over seven to 21 days), a decrease in deaths, a reduction in areas with active transmission, the majority of new cases originating from contacts already identified, and a high rate of contact tracing, as well as dignified and safe burials.

Early last month, Jean Kaseya, the director general of the African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, visited Bunia – capital of Ituri and a centre of the current Ebola outbreak – and said then that there was no way of knowing when the peak might be reached but that containment and contact tracing were still not effective enough.

Kaseya said: “A large portion of the mortality – 60 to 70% of deaths – comes from the community. The list of contacts we have just keeps growing. Epidemiologists say we’ve reached the peak when all cases come from the list of contacts.”

In Rwampara, a town in Ituri, people are exhausted from the past few months of living with the dread of the disease. Léa Munyere, 36, a mother of four, said she was relieved that the health authorities had announced that Ebola was under control. Two of her close friends had died and she was still struggling to come to terms with the loss, she said.

“We hope the disease will soon be declared over. It has robbed us of the people we cherish so much since it was first reported,” she said. “We just want to get back to our normal lives.”

world.title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
world.snippet: St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans Inside the Great Hall of ...
world.content:
Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.

The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.

The Register of British Slave Traders, a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries.

It reveals how wealthy individuals, often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added.

The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to St Barts who are directly linked to this history.

Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing.

Phillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”.

Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits.

The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

The 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings.

Others commemorated at St Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register. William Prichard, once president of St Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678.

Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statue at the Museum of the Home in Hoxton.

These connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including St Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor.

His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to St Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713.

After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants.

The private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70.

He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to St Barts after his death in 1688.

Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, St Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital.

Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare.

St Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report.

A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations.

“As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.”

A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative.

world.title: Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO
world.snippet: Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirds The fortune of Africa’s riches...
world.content:
The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering.

If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth.

Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October.

The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn).

That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors.

Responding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.”

Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar. He started his company in the late 1970s with a loan from his maternal grandfather, who was a member of one of west Africa’s all-time richest families, the Dantatas.

His recent move into the petroleum sector led to Nigeria becoming a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time. Prior to the opening of the $20bn Dangote refinery on the outskirts of Lagos in January 2024, the country had relied on exporting crude and importing refined petroleum for domestic use, while expending billions to subsidise fuel costs and inject life into its colonial-era refineries.

The Dangote refinery now has a capacity of 700,000 barrels a day and is expected to double that by the end of the decade. This year, it has benefited from disruptions in supply across the globe as a result of the war in Iran. The Brent crude benchmark touched $108 a barrel on Monday, after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline.

Dangote has said he will use profits from his Lagos oil refinery to spur continental growth and curb Africa’s reliance on foreign goods. His ambitious plan is to build a $100bn industrial empire centred on heavy manufacturing and regional infrastructure. Key to this is a planned $17bn energy complex in the Kenyan island town of Lamu with an oil-refining capacity of 700,000 barrels a day, to boost the region’s energy security.

“We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony in Lagos on 7 September. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.”

After the ceremony, Dangote’s fellow Nigerian billionaire, the banker Tony Elumelu, called the IPO “a landmark moment for Nigeria and a huge milestone for Africa”.

world.title: Burial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throne
world.snippet: Royal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba ...
world.content:
Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠a bitter succession battle behind ​it.

Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.

Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three. Images of the toddler king wearing a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.

He died last month at 34 ⁠in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.

Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the ​British colonial era and are regarded as bulwarks of traditional identity ‌and heritage.

At a church service before ‌the burial, Oyo, who became a UN goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and Aids, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.

“Although ‌he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun,” said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.

Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo’s casket through the streets of the kingdom’s capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.

The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo’s coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.

A committee consisting of members ‌of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo’s cousin, Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.

But the late king’s immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called ​for in his will. Oyo never married and was not known to have any children until the kingdom’s prime minister said in the statement announcing his death that he had a son.

Supporters of Kijanangoma’s succession say Oyo’s family has not been able to produce basic information about the purported son.

A source with knowledge of crisis talks over the matter said Ugandan authorities had successfully pushed through Kijanangoma’s succession on Friday. A government spokesperson could not be reached for comment.

The archbishop of the ⁠Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba Mugalu, called for unity.

“Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict,” he ​told mourners. “It can even destroy the legacy ​of the king we are mourning.”

Oyo himself took the throne after a protracted succession battle that finished in court.

In ​addition to his ceremonial responsibilities and campaigning ‌against HIV and Aids, ​Oyo cultivated close ties with former ​Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whom he named a special adviser to the monarch. Gaddafi donated money towards refurbishment of the royal palace.

The 56-year-old Kijanangoma, who maintained a low profile as the succession battle played out, has been described by fellow Ugandan journalists as quiet and humble.

Besides the throne, the new king will inherit a considerable royal estate including swathes of land and sizeable cash payouts from the central government.
